sources.title: Visit the Lingaraj Temple in Bhubaneswar | Incredible India
sources.publisherOrAuthority: Ministry of Tourism, Government of India (Incredible India)
sources.claimScope: Eleventh-century commissioning by King Jajati Keshari of the Somavamshi dynasty and the tradition of worship on the site from the seventh century; height of 180 feet and complex of over 40 acres; the four sections vimana, jagamohana, nata mandira and bhoga mandapa; sandstone and laterite construction; joint Shaiva-Vaishnava dedication; Swayambhu lingam of 8 feet diameter and 8 inches height; the restriction of entry to Hindus and the elevated viewing platform for other visitors; stated opening hours of 07:00 to 19:00; Mahashivaratri, Ashokashtami and Chandan Yatra as the major festivals.
sources.reliabilityNote: National tourism ministry page, undated. The single 07:00-19:00 window is a simplification of a temple that in practice opens earlier and observes ritual closures; treat as needing recheck.

sources.title: Lingaraja Temple — Wikipedia
sources.claimScope: Attribution of the late eleventh-century construction to Somavamshi king Yayati I (1025-1040) or his successors; the descending-height arrangement of the four Deula-style components; approximately 150 smaller shrines; Vaishnava elements introduced in the Ganga period, including Vaishnava doorkeepers; the underground stream said to feed the Bindusagar tank; the viewing platform beside the wall, originally built for Viceroy Curzon; joint maintenance by the Archaeological Survey of India and the Temple Trust Board; Shivaratri attendance of over 200,000 and the Rukuna Rath procession at Ashokashtami.
sources.reliabilityNote: Tertiary source, used for history, administration and festival background rather than for timings.

identity.spiritualSignificanceShort: Lingaraja is the presiding shrine of the old temple city of Bhubaneswar and enshrines a swayambhu lingam described as about eight feet across and eight inches high. Worship here is distinctively syncretic: the deity is honoured as Harihara, joining Shiva and Vishnu, and the temple carries Vaishnava iconography introduced under the Ganga dynasty alongside its Shaiva core. The temple is regarded as the culmination of the Kalinga school of temple architecture.
sacredClassifications: Harihara shrine — joint Shaiva and Vaishnava worship

governance.founderPatron: Attributed to the Somavamshi king Yayati I (Jajati Keshari), or to his successors
governance.managingAuthority: Maintained jointly by the Archaeological Survey of India and the temple's Trust Board

narrative.documentedHistory:
The temple is dated to the late eleventh century and is attributed to the Somavamshi king Yayati I, known also as Jajati Keshari, or to his immediate successors; tradition holds that the site was in worship considerably earlier. It is built in sandstone and laterite and represents the mature phase of the Kalinga school of temple architecture in Bhubaneswar.

Although the presiding deity is Shiva as Lingaraja, the temple carries a marked Vaishnava overlay introduced during the Ganga dynasty period, including Vaishnava doorkeepers, reflecting the rising prominence of the Jagannath cult in Odisha. The deity is accordingly worshipped as Harihara, the union of Hari and Hara.

The temple compound is closed to non-Hindus. A raised viewing platform stands beside the boundary wall, originally built so that Viceroy Curzon could see the temple; it remains the point from which visitors who may not enter view the complex.
narrative.architectureStyle: Kalinga (Deula) style; the four components stand in descending height — vimana (sanctum tower, about 180 feet), jagamohana (assembly hall), natamandira (festival hall) and bhoga-mandapa (hall of offerings)
narrative.sacredTank: Bindusagar, the tank north of the temple; an underground stream originating at the temple is said to feed it, and its water is held to be healing

visitingInfo.entryRules: Entry to the temple compound is restricted to Hindus. Visitors who may not enter can see the complex from an elevated viewing platform beside the boundary wall, built originally for Viceroy Curzon and still in use for this purpose.
visitingInfo.officialContactNote: The single 07:00-19:00 window published by the Ministry of Tourism is an approximation; the temple observes its own ritual closures during the day and extends hours on festival days. Confirm current darshan hours locally, and note that Shivaratri and Ashokashtami substantially change access.

openingHours.notes: As published by the Ministry of Tourism. This is a simplified single window and does not reflect intra-day ritual closures or festival-day extensions; the directory's previously recorded split morning and evening sessions were not confirmed by any source opened.
